terms.def: The tall flight of exterior steps leading up to a rowhouse's main entrance on the parlor floor.
terms.spot: Steps rising roughly a full story above the sidewalk, usually with iron or stone railings. From the Dutch stoep.
ex: West 76th Street between Columbus Ave and Central Park West, Upper West Side

terms.def: The small fenced or sunken space between the sidewalk and a rowhouse's front wall.
terms.spot: An iron fence and gate at the sidewalk line, often with steps down to the basement door tucked under the stoop.
ex: Side streets of the Upper West Side

credit.title: File:A bold face 266 West 11th Street (1887), Greenwich Village, New York (50244861407).jpg
credit.artist: Spencer Means from New York City, USA

terms.def: A raised basement just a few steps below sidewalk level, with its own entrance beside or under the stoop.
terms.spot: Windows partly above the sidewalk, a door under the stoop. Often marketed as the "garden level" or "garden duplex".
ex: Most Italianate brownstones in Harlem and Park Slope

terms.def: The projecting molding that crowns the top of a facade, sheltering the wall below.
terms.spot: Look at the roofline: on brownstone rows it's a deep overhang on brackets, usually pressed metal or wood painted to match.
ex: The heavy crowning cornice of the Flatiron Building, 175 Fifth Ave

terms.def: The horizontal band just below the cornice, often decorated or pierced by small attic windows.
terms.spot: The flat strip between the top-floor windows and the cornice's overhang.
ex: Greek Revival rows on Washington Square North

terms.def: The full horizontal band carried by columns: architrave at the bottom, frieze in the middle, cornice on top.
terms.spot: On a classical temple front, everything between the column tops and the pediment.
ex: Federal Hall National Memorial, 26 Wall St
New York Stock Exchange, 18 Broad St

terms.def: The lowest band of an entablature, resting directly on the columns; also the molded frame around a door or window.
terms.spot: Indoors: the casing around a doorway. Outdoors: the plain beam right above the capitals.
ex: Door surrounds in Greek Revival rowhouses on Washington Square North

terms.def: A row of small, closely spaced rectangular blocks under a cornice, like a row of teeth.
terms.spot: A regular comb of little blocks just under the cornice's lip.
ex: Cornices of Federal and Greek Revival houses in Greenwich Village

terms.def: Ornamental scroll-shaped brackets set horizontally under the overhang of a cornice.
terms.spot: Larger and farther apart than dentils, curling like a sideways S; common on Beaux-Arts and Renaissance Revival cornices.

credit.title: File:Madison Co CH KY detail modillions.JPG

terms.def: Projecting supports, real or decorative, holding up a cornice, window hood or balcony.
terms.spot: Tall scrolls under a brownstone cornice, usually in pairs or evenly spaced. The signature of Italianate rows.
ex: Italianate brownstones throughout Park Slope and the Upper West Side

credit.title: File:American Exchange Bank Building, Pinckney Street and Washington Avenue, Madison, WI (52734375703).jpg
credit.artist: Warren LeMay from Covington, KY, United States

terms.def: A block of stone or brick projecting from a wall to support something above it.
terms.spot: Stepped-out brick courses under a parapet (corbelling) or a stone block under an oriel or balcony.
ex: Corbelled brick cornices on Lower East Side tenements

terms.def: The horizontal beam or stone spanning the top of a window or door opening.
terms.spot: A single flat stone over each window. Brownstone and Greek Revival houses often have plain stone lintels against brick.
ex: Greek Revival rowhouses in the Greenwich Village Historic District

credit.title: File:Dr. Bernard Bartow House, Buffalo, New York - 20220302.jpg

terms.def: The horizontal ledge at the bottom of a window opening, sloped to shed rain.
terms.spot: The stone shelf under the window, often projecting on small brackets on brownstones.

credit.title: File:Windows of 109 Washington Street -- Image c. 2012..JPG

terms.def: A projecting molded crown over a window, shedding water and adding ornament.
terms.spot: A heavy carved cap above each brownstone window, often arched or with a pediment shape on little brackets.
ex: Italianate rows in Harlem's Mount Morris Park Historic District

terms.def: A shallow arch whose curve is a segment of a circle, less than a half-circle.
terms.spot: Gently curved tops on windows and doors; common on Italianate brownstones and tenement windows.
ex: Doorways of Italianate brownstones in Fort Greene

terms.def: A full semicircular arch, as in Roman and Romanesque building.
terms.spot: Windows and doorways topped by a full half-circle; heavy versions mark Romanesque Revival.

terms.def: The central wedge-shaped stone at the top of an arch, often enlarged or carved.
terms.spot: The one stone at the arch's crown that sticks out or carries a face or scroll.
ex: Window arches of Renaissance Revival apartment houses on Riverside Drive

terms.def: The wedge-shaped stones or bricks that together form an arch.
terms.spot: The fan of individual blocks radiating around an arch, sometimes in alternating colors.
ex: Arched entrances of Romanesque Revival rowhouses in Park Slope

credit.title: File:Old College, University of Edinburgh courtyard facade detail.jpg

terms.def: A low triangular gable, or a curved (segmental) version, crowning a portico, door or window.
terms.spot: Triangle over the front of a temple-like building, or small triangles and arcs over windows.
ex: New York Stock Exchange, 18 Broad St

terms.def: A porch with a roof held up by columns, usually leading to the main entrance.
terms.spot: A columned front porch, often with a pediment on top.
ex: Federal Hall National Memorial, 26 Wall St

credit.title: File:Federal Hall (48126566178).jpg
credit.artist: Ajay Suresh from New York, NY, USA

terms.def: The plainest classical column: no base (Greek) and a simple cushion-shaped capital.
terms.spot: Thick columns with plain, flat-topped capitals. Think Greek Revival porches.
ex: Federal Hall National Memorial, 26 Wall St

terms.def: The classical column whose capital ends in a pair of scrolls called volutes.
terms.spot: Look for the two spiral scrolls at the top, like a rolled sheet of paper.
ex: Lower colonnade of 55 Wall Street (former Merchants' Exchange)

credit.title: File:National City Bank Building 55 Wall Street.jpg

terms.def: The most ornate classical column, its capital carved with acanthus leaves.
terms.spot: Leafy, bell-shaped tops sprouting small scrolls at the corners.
ex: New York Stock Exchange, 18 Broad St

terms.def: A flat, shallow column projecting slightly from a wall, purely decorative.
terms.spot: Looks like a column pressed flat against the facade, with a base and capital; frames doorways in Greek Revival houses.

terms.def: A round column partly embedded in a wall, so only half or three-quarters stands free.
terms.spot: Round, unlike a pilaster, but attached to the facade.
ex: Classical bank and civic facades of the early 1900s

credit.title: File:The Maison Carrée, 1st century BCE Corinthian temple commissioned by Marcus Agrippa, Nemausus (Nîmes, France) (14562056828).jpg

terms.def: Dressed stones or blocks laid at the corners of a building, alternating long and short.
terms.spot: A zipper-like pattern of blocks running up the corners, often in a contrasting color.
ex: Corners of Georgian and Beaux-Arts mansions on the Upper East Side

terms.def: Masonry cut with deep joints or rough faces so the stones read as massive and strong, usually on the ground floor.
terms.spot: Bold horizontal grooves or rough boulder-like stone at the base of a building.
ex: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, 33 Liberty St

credit.title: File:Federal Reserve Bank of New York Building 003.jpg

terms.def: A horizontal band of stone or brick across a facade, usually marking a floor line. Also called a stringcourse.
terms.spot: A continuous ledge or stripe running across the building between floors.
ex: Prewar apartment houses on West End Avenue

terms.def: A bay window projecting from an upper floor, supported on brackets or corbels, that doesn't reach the ground.
terms.spot: A box of windows hanging off the facade with nothing beneath it.
ex: Rowhouses of the Riverside–West End Historic District

credit.title: File:Maison 8 rue des Pucelles à Strasbourg (2).jpg

terms.def: A projecting window bay that rises from the ground or foundation.
terms.spot: A projecting bay with walls that run all the way down to the sidewalk or areaway.
ex: Bowed and angled bays on Park Slope rowhouses

credit.title: File:ROW HOUSES IN BROOKLYN, NEW YORK CITY. THE INNER CITY TODAY IS AN ABSOLUTE CONTRADICTION TO THE MAIN STREAM AMERICA... - NARA - 555912.jpg

terms.def: A double-pitched roof with a very steep lower slope, nearly a wall, pierced by dormers. Signature of the Second Empire style.
terms.spot: A steep slate or copper roof that adds an extra story, with dormer windows poking out.

terms.def: A window set into a small roofed projection that pokes out of a sloped roof.
terms.spot: Little roofed windows on a pitched or mansard roof. Federal houses have them on their peaked roofs.
ex: Federal houses in the Charlton–King–Vandam Historic District

credit.title: File:Fenêtre sur le toit du Palais de Justice.JPG

terms.def: A low wall rising above the roofline.
terms.spot: The wall that keeps going past the roof, sometimes stepped, crenellated or topped with a balustrade.
ex: Tenements and loft buildings across SoHo

credit.title: File:Wall Street, Stockade Historic District, Kingston, New York - 20200907 - 02 (Winne and Winchell Building).jpg

terms.def: A railing made of a row of short posts (balusters) topped by a rail.
terms.spot: A row of vase-shaped posts along a roofline, terrace, balcony or stair.
ex: Rooflines of Beaux-Arts buildings on Fifth Avenue

terms.def: An open-sided gallery or arcade recessed into a building and open to the air on one side.
terms.spot: A roofed, columned open space set back into the facade, often on upper floors.
ex: Upper-story loggias on Renaissance Revival apartment houses
Recessed loggia terraces of new condos such as The Park Loggia, 15 West 61st St

credit.title: File:New York State Fairgrounds - loggia between Dairy Products and Science & Industry Buildings - 20210321.jpg

terms.def: A row of arches carried on columns or piers.
terms.spot: A rhythm of repeated arches along a ground floor or across a facade.
ex: Stacked arcades of the Haughwout Building, 488 Broadway

terms.def: A semicircular or elliptical window over a door, often with radiating muntins like a fan.
terms.spot: A half-moon of glass over the front door, a hallmark of Federal-style houses.
ex: Federal rowhouses in the Charlton–King–Vandam Historic District

credit.title: File:Doorway- Tredwell House, 29 East 4th Street, Manhattan (NYPL b13668355-1219143).jpg

terms.def: Narrow vertical windows flanking a door.
terms.spot: Thin glass panels on each side of the front door; Greek Revival doorways pair them with a rectangular transom.
ex: Greek Revival doorways on Washington Square North

terms.def: On a skyscraper, the panel between the top of one window and the sill of the one above; in an arch, the roughly triangular space beside its curve.
terms.spot: The decorated or metal panels stacked between windows in vertical strips, a key Art Deco surface.
ex: Aluminum spandrels of the Empire State Building, 350 Fifth Ave

terms.def: An upper-floor step-back required by the 1916 Zoning Resolution so light reaches the street, giving towers their "wedding cake" profile.
terms.spot: Floors stepping in as the building rises, often with terraces on each step.
ex: Prewar towers along Central Park West

terms.def: The decorative top of a tower, designed to be seen from far away.
terms.spot: Look up past the main shaft: terraced arches, spires, lanterns or temples.
ex: Twin towers of the San Remo, 145 Central Park West

terms.def: A carved spout, often a creature, that throws rainwater off a roof. Purely ornamental versions are grotesques.
terms.spot: Creatures projecting from cornices and setbacks.
ex: Steel eagle heads on the Chrysler Building, 405 Lexington Ave

terms.def: An ornament capping the top of a spire, gable, post or roof peak.
terms.spot: A knob, urn or spike at the very top point.
ex: Spires of St. Patrick's Cathedral, Fifth Ave at 50th St

terms.def: External iron balconies and ladders, required on tenements from the 1860s as an emergency exit.
terms.spot: Zigzag iron stairs or stacked balconies across the front of tenements and loft buildings.
ex: Tenement blocks of the Lower East Side

credit.title: File:Fire escape, West 10th Street, Greenwich Village, NYC.jpg

terms.def: A wooden rooftop tank that stores water for buildings taller than about six stories, beyond what city water pressure reaches.
terms.spot: Barrel-shaped cedar or redwood tanks with cone hats on steel legs. A few firms, like Rosenwach, still build them.

credit.title: File:Rooftop water towers in SoHo, Manhattan.jpg

terms.def: A non-load-bearing outer skin of glass and metal hung on a building's frame.
terms.spot: A continuous grid of glass and mullions with no visible masonry holding anything up.

terms.def: The principal floor of a grand house, raised one story above the ground and given the tallest windows.
terms.spot: One floor up, with the biggest windows, balconies or most ornament. The parlor floor is New York's version.

terms.def: A building front of prefabricated cast-iron parts bolted together, popular from the 1850s to the 1880s.
terms.spot: Repeated columns and arches with crisp, identical detail; a magnet sticks. SoHo has the world's largest concentration.

credit.title: File:E.V. Haughwout Building, Broadway, New York.jpg

terms.def: The main floor of a rowhouse, reached by the stoop, with the tallest ceilings and grandest rooms.
terms.spot: One flight up from the sidewalk: double parlors, ornate plaster, the best mantels.

terms.def: Two connected front and rear parlors, typically divided by pocket doors or a columned screen.
terms.spot: Two matched rooms, each with a mantel, opening into each other through a wide doorway.

terms.def: A row of rooms whose doorways line up, so you can see straight through all of them.
terms.spot: Stand in one room and look through a series of aligned doors.
ex: Fifth Avenue prewar co-ops along the park

credit.title: File:Doorways of Enfilade inside Ducal Palace, Urbino.jpg

terms.def: Sliding doors that disappear into a cavity in the wall.
terms.spot: A wide opening between parlors with brass pulls showing at the door edges.

credit.title: File:POCKET DOOR BETWEEN HALL AND DINING ROOM, IN OPEN POSITION - Arthur Marston House, 3575 Seventh Avenue, San Diego, San Diego County, CA HABS CAL,37-SANDI,21-2.tif

terms.def: A round or oval plaster ornament on the ceiling, where a gas chandelier once hung.
terms.spot: A circle of plaster leaves or rings in the center of the ceiling.
ex: Parlors of brownstones in Park Slope and Harlem

terms.def: Molding running along the top of a wall where it meets the ceiling.
terms.spot: Deep layered plaster at the ceiling edge; in brownstones it's often called the plaster cornice.
ex: Prewar apartments and brownstone parlors citywide

credit.title: File:Crown molding (5098483884).jpg
credit.artist: The Finishing Company Richmond Va from Richmond,Virginia, United States

terms.def: A ceiling that curves into the wall instead of meeting it at a sharp angle.
terms.spot: A smooth concave sweep where wall becomes ceiling.

terms.def: A ceiling divided into a grid of sunken panels.
terms.spot: Recessed square or octagonal boxes overhead, framed by beams.
ex: Libraries of Upper East Side townhouses

terms.def: A ceiling crossed by exposed or decorative beams running one direction.
terms.spot: Parallel beams, not a grid. Tudor and Arts and Crafts rooms love them.
ex: Tudor Revival rooms in prewar co-ops

credit.title: File:Decorated ceiling beams in the Dining Room at Godolphin House - geograph.org.uk - 4991380.jpg

terms.def: A narrow molding a foot or two below the ceiling, made for hanging pictures on hooks and wire.
terms.spot: A thin strip running around the room, well below the crown molding.
ex: Prewar apartments throughout the Upper West Side

terms.def: A horizontal molding around a room at about chair-back height, to protect the wall.
terms.spot: A strip about three feet off the floor, often capping wainscoting.
ex: Dining rooms of prewar classic sixes

terms.def: Paneling covering the lower part of a wall.
terms.spot: Wood or plaster panels from the floor up to a rail at about waist height.
ex: Entry halls and dining rooms in prewar co-ops

credit.title: File:To bring the church back to its 1913 appearance, contractors stripped the dark, dirty finish from the wainscoting. This image (4bc03e74-b200-4eb6-86df-31bdf3f5a27c).jpg

terms.def: Carved, often painted or gilded, French wood paneling covering whole walls.
terms.spot: Floor-to-ceiling panels with curving frames, Louis XV or XVI style.
ex: Period rooms in the Frick Collection, 1 East 70th St

terms.def: Parquet with rectangular blocks laid in a zigzag where ends meet at right angles, staggered.
terms.spot: Ends of the boards butt against the sides of their neighbors, like a broken zigzag.

credit.title: File:Herringbone parquet diff 16k (Anonymous Bob and Jandre van Heerden via Poly Haven).png
credit.artist: Anonymous Bob and Jandre van Heerden (Poly Haven)

terms.def: Parquet with boards cut at an angle so they meet in a clean point, forming continuous Vs.
terms.spot: A crisp unbroken V down the room. Ends are mitered, unlike herringbone.
ex: New luxury condos and Parisian-style renovations

terms.def: A decorative band of contrasting wood set around the edge of a floor.
terms.spot: A stripe or Greek-key pattern of darker wood framing the room.
ex: Brownstone parlors and prewar living rooms

terms.def: Pictures or patterns made of shaped veneers of different woods fitted together.
terms.spot: Flowers, stars or scrolls made of contrasting wood on a floor or furniture.
ex: Gilded Age mansions such as the Frick Collection

credit.title: File:Sòl de marqueteria de l'oratori del palau ducal, Gandia.jpg

terms.def: The large post at the bottom (or turns) of a staircase that anchors the handrail.
terms.spot: The heavy carved post where the banister starts.

terms.def: The short posts between a stair's handrail and its steps.
terms.spot: The row of turned spindles under the handrail.

terms.def: A skylight, often with an oval opening below it, lighting a rowhouse stair from the roof.
terms.spot: Look straight up the stair hall: glass at the top floor, sometimes over an oval well.

terms.def: A window above a door, often hinged to open, for air and light between rooms or into a hall.
terms.spot: A rectangular pane over interior or entry doors.

terms.def: A small entry room between an outer and inner set of doors.
terms.spot: Two sets of doors at a brownstone entrance, often with an encaustic tile floor between.

terms.def: Tile with a pattern made of different colored clays inlaid, not painted, so it doesn't wear off.
terms.spot: Geometric multi-colored tile floors in vestibules and hallways.

credit.title: File:Gladstone encaustic tile gallery 3869.JPG
credit.artist: Photograph by Clem Rutter, Rochester, Kent. (www.clemrutter.net).

terms.def: Small white six-sided ceramic floor tile, standard in prewar bathrooms.
terms.spot: Tiny white hexagons, sometimes with a black border or flower pattern.

terms.def: Glazed 3×6-inch rectangular ceramic tile, introduced in the city's first subway stations in 1904.
terms.spot: White rectangular tiles in a running-bond pattern, usually on walls.

terms.def: An Italianate fireplace surround of white or colored marble with a round-arched opening and a carved keystone.
terms.spot: The curved fireplace opening is the tell; Greek Revival mantels are square instead.

credit.title: File:Arlington House - State Dining Room - fireplace mantel - 2011.jpg

terms.def: A Greek Revival fireplace surround: plain columns or pilasters holding a flat shelf, often black or gray marble.
terms.spot: Square opening, severe and architectural.

credit.title: File:Fireplace, West Parlor, Main House, McLeod Plantation, James Island, Charleston, SC.jpg

terms.def: A tall mirror set between two windows (on the pier) or over a mantel, often in a gilded frame.
terms.spot: Floor-to-ceiling gilt mirrors in brownstone parlors.

credit.title: File:Mirror and pier table, V&A London 02.jpg

terms.def: Folding wooden shutters that fold into recesses beside the windows.
terms.spot: Deep window jambs with panels that unfold across the glass.

terms.def: In a prewar apartment, a formal entry hall large enough for furniture and art, from which rooms open.
terms.spot: A room, not a hallway, between the front door and the living room.
ex: Rosario Candela co-ops such as 740 Park Ave

credit.title: File:Interior entrance of the Biltmore Apartments on E Loretta Pl, 1925 (SEATTLE 2533).jpg

terms.def: A service room between kitchen and dining room, with cabinets, a sink and a swinging door.
terms.spot: A passage-like room lined with glass-front cabinets.

credit.title: File:The Butler's Pantry, Raby Castle - geograph.org.uk - 7268794.jpg

terms.def: A small hand-pulled elevator for carrying food and goods between floors.
terms.spot: A little door in a wall at counter height, often painted shut.

credit.title: File:Dumbwaiter at Biltmore House, Asheville, North Carolina.jpg

terms.def: A living room set a step or two below the surrounding floor.
terms.spot: Steps down from the gallery into the living room; common in 1950s–60s postwar buildings.
ex: Postwar co-ops on the Upper East Side

terms.def: A Victorian embossed wallcovering made of linseed paste, painted to look like carved plaster or leather.
terms.spot: Raised patterns on walls or dados in stair halls, often under layers of paint.

terms.def: The city's earliest surviving rowhouse style: modest red-brick houses two and a half stories tall with peaked roofs.
terms.spot: Flemish-bond brick, a pitched roof with dormers, a low stoop, and a doorway with a fanlight.

terms.def: Red-brick rowhouses with flat roofs and temple-inspired doorways, reflecting a fashion for ancient Greece.
terms.spot: Three full stories with a flat roof and simple cornice, a rectangular transom and sidelights around the door, framed by columns or pilasters.

terms.def: A medieval revival using pointed arches, tracery and verticality, mostly for churches.
terms.spot: Pointed-arch windows and doors, spires, buttresses, drip moldings.
ex: Trinity Church, Broadway at Wall St
St. Patrick's Cathedral, Fifth Ave at 50th St

terms.def: The classic brownstone: tall stooped rowhouses modeled on Italian palazzos, faced in brownstone.
terms.spot: High stoop with cast-iron railings, heavy bracketed cornice, arched or segmental windows with carved hoods, double doors in a deep arched doorway.
ex: Mount Morris Park Historic District, Harlem

terms.def: A style borrowed from Napoleon III's Paris, defined by the mansard roof.
terms.spot: Mansard roof with dormers on top of an otherwise Italianate building.

credit.title: File:Mansard - Saratoga Springs, NY - Michael Nolan House (1).jpg

terms.def: A late brownstone style with crisp, angular, machine-cut ornament.
terms.spot: Incised lines grooved into the stone, stylized angular brackets, flatter and more geometric than Italianate.
ex: Rowhouses of the Upper West Side–Central Park West Historic District

terms.def: A picturesque, deliberately irregular style that mixes materials, gables, towers and textures.
terms.spot: Asymmetry: turrets, gables, bay windows, terra cotta panels and several kinds of brick on one facade.
ex: Henderson Place Historic District, East End Ave at 86th St

terms.def: A heavy, massive style built on round arches and rough-faced stone, often called Richardsonian after H.H. Richardson.
terms.spot: Wide round arches over entrances, rock-faced stone, deep-set windows, squat columns.

credit.title: File:Romanesque Revival - New York, NY - Astor Library (1).jpg

terms.def: Buildings modeled on Italian Renaissance palazzos: symmetrical, layered and restrained.
terms.spot: A rusticated base, an even middle and a big cornice, with tidy rows of windows and classical trim.

terms.def: Grand, exuberant classicism taught at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris.
terms.spot: Pale stone, monumental scale, paired columns, rich sculpture, balustrades and sometimes a mansard roof.
ex: New York Public Library, Fifth Ave at 42nd St
terms.wiki: New York Public Library Main Branch

credit.title: File:New York Public Library Main Branch facade.jpg

terms.def: Jazz Age modernity: stepped setbacks, strong verticals and stylized geometric ornament.
terms.spot: Zigzags, chevrons, sunbursts, metal spandrels and corner windows; masses stepping up to a crown.

terms.def: Plain brick apartment slabs built in the housing boom after World War II.
terms.spot: White or red brick, little ornament, balconies, ribbon or corner windows, lower ceilings than prewar.
ex: Second and Third Avenue towers on the Upper East Side

terms.def: Modernism with no ornament at all: a pure volume of glass and steel.
terms.spot: Glass curtain walls, flat tops, regular grids, often a plaza in front.

terms.def: A reaction against glass boxes that brings back historic forms, often with wit.
terms.spot: Exaggerated classical shapes, pediments and arches in new materials, playful tops.

terms.def: New buildings that revive prewar limestone grandeur, led by Robert A.M. Stern.
terms.spot: New limestone towers with setbacks, classical trim and prewar-style layouts.

terms.def: Today's luxury towers: engineered slenderness, sculptural form and glass or terra cotta skins.
terms.spot: Extremely thin towers, irregular or twisting massing, cantilevers, floor-to-ceiling glass.

terms.def: A brown Triassic sandstone, much of it quarried in Portland, Connecticut, and the dominant rowhouse facing from the 1850s to the 1880s.
terms.spot: Chocolate-brown stone that flakes and spalls with age. Usually a thin veneer over brick, so restorations often use tinted stucco.
ex: Rows in Park Slope, Bedford-Stuyvesant and Harlem

terms.def: A pale, fine-grained sedimentary stone, mostly from Indiana, that carves crisply; the dress of Beaux-Arts and prewar luxury buildings.
terms.spot: Smooth cream or buff stone with sharp carving. Limestone townhouses stand out in brownstone rows from the 1890s on.
ex: Fifth Avenue mansions of the Upper East Side

terms.def: Metamorphic limestone that takes a polish; in New York, much of it white Tuckahoe and Inwood marble.
terms.spot: Brilliant white stone with faint veining; outdoors it weathers to a sugary surface.
ex: Sun Building (former A.T. Stewart store), 280 Broadway

terms.def: A hard, speckled igneous stone used for bases, steps and heavy structures.
terms.spot: Salt-and-pepper or pink speckles; often the first floor or the stoop, under softer stone.
ex: Base of the Federal Reserve Bank, 33 Liberty St

credit.title: File:Base of the Brooklyn-side tower of the Brooklyn Bridge, low-angle view, New York City.jpg

terms.def: Brickwork with long sides (stretchers) and short ends (headers) alternating within every course.
terms.spot: Each row goes long-short-long-short, often with darker glazed headers. The giveaway of a Federal house.
ex: Federal houses in the Charlton–King–Vandam Historic District

terms.def: Brickwork showing only long sides, each course offset by half a brick.
terms.spot: No headers at all. Usually means a brick veneer over a steel or concrete frame, so 20th century.
ex: Postwar apartment buildings across the Upper East Side

credit.title: File:Solna Brick wall Stretcher bond variation1.jpg

terms.def: Brickwork with a row of headers every five to seven courses of stretchers. Also called American bond.
terms.spot: Mostly long sides, with a header stripe every sixth row or so; typical of side walls and tenements.
ex: Side walls of 19th-century tenements on the Lower East Side

terms.def: Long, thin brick that stresses horizontal lines, popular around 1890–1915 and again with modernists.
terms.spot: Bricks noticeably flatter and longer than usual, often tan or buff.
ex: Turn-of-the-century townhouses in the Upper East Side Historic District

terms.def: Fired clay molded into ornament or wall cladding, lighter and cheaper than carved stone.
terms.spot: Repeating ornament with crisp identical copies, sometimes glazed to look like stone.

terms.def: Iron poured into molds, used for prefabricated facades, columns, railings and stoop newels.
terms.spot: Repeated, sharp ornament painted to look like stone; often with rust where the paint chips.

terms.def: Thin galvanized sheet metal stamped into ornament, used for cornices, bay windows and ceilings.
terms.spot: Brownstone cornices are usually this, not stone. Indoors, it's the "tin ceiling".

credit.title: File:Old Gee How Oak Tin Family Association at Wing Luke Museum detail 02 (ceiling).jpg

terms.def: Thin interlocking tiles laid in layers to form self-supporting vaults, patented by Rafael Guastavino in the 1880s.
terms.spot: Herringbone-patterned tile vaults overhead with no visible supports.
ex: Grand Central Oyster Bar, Grand Central Terminal

terms.def: A blue-gray sandstone split into large flat slabs, used for sidewalks, steps and garden paths.
terms.spot: Big, uneven gray slabs on old sidewalks in front of brownstones.
ex: Sidewalks of Brooklyn Heights and Greenwich Village

terms.def: The green coating copper forms as it weathers outdoors.
terms.spot: Pale green roofs, dormers, cornices and spires.
ex: Copper dormers and cresting on The Plaza, 768 Fifth Ave

credit.title: File:Palais Garnier - Close-up of green copper dome with eagle sculptures and bullseye window.jpg

terms.def: Brick with a fired glassy finish that resists dirt; white versions defined postwar "white-brick" buildings.
terms.spot: Shiny brick that reflects light, often white or pale gray.

terms.def: An attached house sharing side walls (party walls) with its neighbors in a continuous row.
terms.spot: Identical or related facades in an unbroken line along the block.

terms.def: In New York usage, any single-family (or small multi-family) house in the city, row or freestanding; originally a rich family's city residence.
terms.spot: Real estate shorthand, often for a wider or grander house.

credit.title: File:East Side windows, Manhattan - Flickr - Spencer Means.jpg
credit.artist: Spencer Means from New York City, USA

terms.def: New York shorthand for almost any 19th-century rowhouse, whether faced in brownstone, brick or limestone.
terms.spot: If someone calls a red-brick Greek Revival house a brownstone, they're using it this way.

credit.title: File:2014 Striver's Row 211-203 W 138 by Bruce Price & Clarence S. Luce.jpg

terms.def: A wall shared by two adjoining buildings, owned jointly.
terms.spot: The side walls of a rowhouse. Ask what's shared before structural work.

terms.def: An apartment that occupies an entire floor of a rowhouse, with windows front and back.
terms.spot: Front and rear exposures in one unit.
ex: Brownstone rentals in Brooklyn and Harlem

terms.def: An apartment whose rooms are lined up one behind the next, with no hallway.
terms.spot: You walk through each room to reach the next, like train cars.
ex: Tenements in the East Village and Greenpoint

terms.def: Walk-up apartment buildings built under the 1879 law, many with a "dumbbell" plan pinched in the middle for an airshaft.
terms.spot: Five or six stories, narrow lot, front fire escape; interior rooms lit by a tiny shaft.

terms.def: Apartment buildings built after the Tenement House Act of 1901, which required larger courts, windows in every room and indoor toilets.
terms.spot: Wider buildings, often on two or more lots, with real courtyards.
ex: Walk-ups in Washington Heights and the South Bronx

terms.def: An open court cut into a building's footprint to bring light and air to inner rooms.
terms.spot: A U, H or E-shaped building plan with an open notch facing the street or rear.
ex: Prewar apartment buildings along Riverside Drive

terms.def: A narrow vertical shaft between or within buildings, meant to ventilate interior rooms.
terms.spot: Windows facing a brick wall a few feet away.
ex: Old-law tenements on the Lower East Side

credit.title: File:Airshaft of a dumbbell tenement, New York City, taken from the roof, ca. 1900 - NARA - 535468.jpg
credit.artist: Unknown authorUnknown author or not provided

terms.def: The first respectable middle-class apartment houses, from the 1870s, borrowed from Paris to overcome the stigma of tenement living.
terms.spot: 1870s–1880s apartment buildings with modest ornament, often with stores at the base.
ex: Stuyvesant Apartments, East 18th St (1870, Richard Morris Hunt; demolished)

terms.def: A building of suites without full kitchens, served by a central kitchen and hotel staff.
terms.spot: Grand early-1900s buildings; many units now have converted kitchens.

terms.def: Built before World War II, typically 1900–1940, prized for thick walls, high ceilings and gracious layouts.
terms.spot: Plaster walls, 9–11 foot ceilings, formal entry gallery, separate dining room, solid hardwood floors.
ex: Classic co-ops on West End Ave and Park Ave

credit.title: File:Cleburne bldg West End Av & 105 St jeh.jpg

terms.def: Built after World War II, roughly 1945–1980, usually with lower ceilings and more open layouts than prewar.
terms.spot: 8-foot ceilings, balconies, through-wall air conditioning sleeves, simple lobbies.
ex: East Side towers along Second and Third Avenues

terms.def: Postwar planning that set apartment towers in open lawns and plazas instead of along the street.
terms.spot: Repeated towers on a superblock with no through streets.

terms.def: Low-rise apartment buildings grouped around shared interior gardens.
terms.spot: Four- to six-story buildings wrapping a private landscaped block interior.

terms.def: A former stable for horses and carriages, often now a house.
terms.spot: Wide arched ground-floor openings where carriage doors were; hayloft doors above.

credit.title: File:1 Sniffen Court - New York City - DSC07759.jpg

terms.def: A small lane of former stables and carriage houses behind grand houses.
terms.spot: A gated, cobbled lane of low buildings.

terms.def: A former manufacturing or warehouse space with high ceilings, big windows and open floors, converted to residential use.
terms.spot: Columns in the middle of the room, 12-foot-plus ceilings, oversized windows, freight elevator.

terms.def: Originally a small structure on a roof; now the top-floor apartment, often with terraces on the setbacks.
terms.spot: Top-floor units set back from the facade, with terraces.
ex: Setback terraces of Central Park West towers

terms.def: The broad lower base of a tower, often lining the street, from which a slimmer tower rises.
terms.spot: A block of a few stories filling the lot, then a narrower tower above.

terms.def: A skyscraper at least 300 meters (about 984 feet) tall.
terms.spot: Billionaires' Row along 57th Street is the densest cluster.

terms.def: An extremely slender tower, very tall relative to its narrow base.
terms.spot: Roughly 10:1 or more height to width. 111 West 57th is about 24:1.

credit.title: File:05 23 2022 Supertall Building 111 West 57th Street from Roof NYC.jpg

terms.def: A tall, narrow building on a small midblock lot, restricted by the 1983 sliver law in many residential districts.
terms.spot: A tower squeezed between low buildings on a lot 45 feet wide or less.
ex: Narrow 1970s–80s towers on Upper East Side side streets

terms.def: Unused development rights above a property that can be sold to an adjoining lot, letting a neighbor build taller.
terms.spot: A tower rising over a low landmark next door often bought that landmark's air rights.
ex: Towers around Grand Central using the terminal's transferred rights

terms.def: A building or area protected by the Landmarks Preservation Commission, created in 1965 after the loss of Penn Station.
terms.spot: Exterior changes need LPC approval; a bronze plaque often marks individual landmarks.
ex: Brooklyn Heights, the city's first historic district (1965)

terms.def: The architect of the most coveted prewar co-ops, famous for intricate duplex and triplex floor plans.
terms.spot: Limestone-based Park and Fifth Avenue co-ops of 1927–1931 with grand galleries and staggered floor levels.

credit.title: File:740 Park Avenue.jpg
credit.artist: Eden, Janine and Jim from New York City

terms.def: Designer of the great twin-towered Central Park West apartment houses; his firm later built many postwar towers.
terms.spot: Prewar towers with ornate crowns, often paired twin towers facing the park.
ex: The San Remo, 145 Central Park West
The El Dorado, 300 Central Park West

credit.title: File:The San Remo from Central Park (51875589159).jpg

terms.def: A prolific designer of early Park and Fifth Avenue luxury apartment buildings.
terms.spot: Dignified Renaissance Revival co-ops from the 1910s and 1920s.

terms.def: The leading American firm of the Gilded Age, masters of Renaissance and classical design.
terms.spot: Refined, scholarly classical buildings in stone and brick.

terms.def: École-trained partners behind some of the city's finest Beaux-Arts landmarks.
terms.spot: Grand white marble or limestone with lavish sculpture.
ex: New York Public Library, Fifth Ave at 42nd St

terms.def: Beaux-Arts firm behind Grand Central Terminal and many Park Avenue apartment houses.
terms.spot: Classical grandeur, from the terminal facade to dignified Park Avenue co-ops.

terms.def: Architect of the Dakota and the Plaza, two of the city's most romantic buildings.
terms.spot: Picturesque rooflines with gables, dormers and mansards.

credit.title: File:The Dakota (48269594271).jpg
credit.artist: Ajay Suresh from New York, NY, USA

terms.def: Architect of the Woolworth Building, the "Cathedral of Commerce" and the world's tallest building from 1913 to 1930.
terms.spot: Gothic-ornamented skyscrapers and monumental Beaux-Arts civic buildings.
ex: Alexander Hamilton U.S. Custom House, 1 Bowling Green

terms.def: The first American trained at the École des Beaux-Arts, who brought the style home.
terms.spot: Grand classical compositions, French-inspired.
ex: Fifth Avenue facade of the Metropolitan Museum of Art
Pedestal of the Statue of Liberty

credit.title: File:Metropolitan Museum of Art (The Met) - Central Park, NYC.jpg

terms.def: Leading Gothic Revival architect of mid-19th-century New York.
terms.spot: Pointed arches, spires and white stone church fronts.
ex: St. Patrick's Cathedral, Fifth Ave at 50th St

terms.def: Architect of the Chrysler Building, Art Deco's showpiece.
terms.spot: Stainless steel, automotive ornament, a terraced sunburst crown.

terms.def: Firm that designed the Empire State Building, built in just over a year.
terms.spot: Limestone and aluminum Deco setbacks rising to a mast.

terms.def: Developer-architect behind the twin-towered Art Deco apartment houses on Central Park West.
terms.spot: Deco twin towers with horizontal bands and corner windows.

terms.def: Modernist master of "less is more"; his only New York building is the Seagram Building.
terms.spot: Bronze-toned steel and glass, set back behind a granite plaza.
ex: Seagram Building, 375 Park Ave (with Philip Johnson)

terms.def: The corporate modernist firm behind Lever House and One World Trade Center.
terms.spot: Crisp glass towers, from 1950s slabs to today's supertalls.
ex: Manhattan House, 200 East 66th St (with Mayer & Whittlesey)

terms.def: Architect who helped launch modernism in America, then led the turn to postmodernism.
terms.spot: From glass modernism to a granite skyscraper with a broken pediment.

terms.def: The leading architect of new classical luxury towers, which revived prewar limestone glamour.
terms.spot: New limestone towers with setbacks, terraces and lanterns on top.

terms.def: Modernist known for pure white and glass, whose Perry Street towers kicked off the far West Village glass condo.
terms.spot: White steel frames and floor-to-ceiling glass.

credit.title: File:Hudson River Park td (2019-04-24) 058 - 173-176 Perry Street, 165 Charles Street.jpg

terms.def: Firm behind some of today's most striking towers, including the world's most slender skyscraper.
terms.spot: Terra cotta and bronze ribs, copper cladding, sky bridges.

terms.def: Danish firm known for bold geometric shapes that combine courtyard living with tower form.
terms.spot: Sloping, twisting or tilted volumes.

terms.def: Swiss firm whose 56 Leonard stacks glass-walled homes like a game of Jenga.
terms.spot: Cantilevered, stacked boxes; inventive facades.

terms.def: Architect of 432 Park Avenue, a stark concrete grid rising nearly 1,400 feet.
terms.spot: A perfect square in plan, with a uniform grid of 10-foot windows.

terms.def: Architect known for rippling, sculptural surfaces.
terms.spot: Stainless steel that folds like fabric, or white glass that billows.
